evidence.evidence_summary: Nature 2026 states dogs were the only domestic animal in Europe before agriculture and were domesticated from grey wolves toward the end of the last Ice Age.
evidence.limitations: Does not resolve exact origin location or first domestication event.

evidence.evidence_summary: Study states where in the world dogs were domesticated and which human groups were involved remain unknown.
evidence.limitations: Addresses current uncertainty, not a mechanism.

evidence.evidence_summary: Reports nuclear and mitochondrial dog genomes from Pınarbaşı ~15,800 years and Gough’s Cave ~14,300 years.
evidence.limitations: Dates refer to sampled remains; not dates of domestication onset.

evidence.evidence_summary: Reports 14,200-year-old Kesslerloch dog with ancestry shared with later dogs and diversification predating it.
evidence.limitations: Does not identify the original wolf population.

evidence.locator: Abstract + sections 'Genetically similar Palaeolithic dogs' and 'Close Palaeolithic human–dog association'
evidence.evidence_summary: Finds genetically similar Palaeolithic dogs across Europe and Anatolia associated with genetically and culturally distinct human groups; exchange/dispersal is inferred.
evidence.limitations: Exact social mechanism of dog transfer cannot be observed directly.
evidence.population_scope: sampled ancient dogs and human contexts

evidence.evidence_summary: States there is no consensus on when, where and how dog domestication occurred, while grey wolves gave rise to dogs.
By 11,000 years ago at least five major ancestry lineages of dogs had diversified.
evidence.limitations: Lineage count depends on sampled ancient genomes and analytical resolution.

evidence.locator: Abstract + sections 'Dog ancestry has eastern wolf affinities' and 'A second source for western dog ancestry'
evidence.evidence_summary: Dogs show stronger affinity to eastern Eurasian ancient wolves and ancestry from at least two wolf-related sources; western-related ancestry contributes to Near Eastern/African and later European dogs.
evidence.limitations: Cannot distinguish all single-vs-multiple domestication scenarios.

evidence.locator: Abstract + 'Dog ancestry has eastern wolf affinities'
evidence.evidence_summary: None of the analysed ancient wolf genomes is a direct match for dog progenitor ancestries.
evidence.limitations: Absence from sampled genomes is not proof that progenitor populations did not exist.
evidence.geographic_scope: Europe, Siberia, North America plus comparative wolves

evidence.evidence_summary: Science 2020 identifies dogs as the first domestic animal.
evidence.limitations: Not a statement about exact domestication location.

evidence.evidence_summary: Bonn-Oberkassel dog is ~14,223 years old, about seven months old, buried with two humans, and showed evidence of severe distemper; authors interpret survival as prolonged human care.
evidence.limitations: Care inference is archaeological interpretation, not direct observation.

evidence.evidence_summary: Authors note domestication reasonably predates the 14.2 ka dog by several millennia to allow observed structure, while saying their data cannot resolve exact origin.
evidence.limitations: Amount of lead time is not directly dated; wording must remain qualified.

evidence.locator: Abstract + sections on commensal scavenger and cross-species adoption hypotheses
evidence.evidence_summary: Review contrasts commensal-scavenging and cross-species-adoption narratives and argues assumptions remain debated.
evidence.limitations: Review author favors adoption interpretation; not consensus proof.

evidence.evidence_summary: Review discusses behavioral/social selection as central to wolf-human domestication scenarios.
evidence.limitations: Mechanistic plausibility is not direct archaeological proof of sequence.

evidence.evidence_summary: Modern dog-owner gaze interactions were associated with an oxytocin positive feedback loop.
evidence.limitations: Modern experimental result cannot establish the original Palaeolithic cause of domestication.

evidence.evidence_summary: Comparative genomics identified dog selection signals in genes related to starch digestion and fat metabolism.
evidence.limitations: Modern-dog genomic signature does not by itself date when every adaptation arose.

evidence.evidence_summary: Ancient European dogs show changing AMY2B copy number; strong modern expansion was not universal in early dogs.
evidence.limitations: Ancient sample set is regionally and temporally limited.

evidence.evidence_summary: Co-analysis of dog and human genomes found several aspects of dog population history mirroring humans.
Study identifies eastern Eurasian dog ancestry influx during the Mesolithic and later ancestry mixtures in Europe.
evidence.limitations: Exact timing and magnitude vary across sampled populations.
